title: The borrowed gloves
text:
Leo had wanted to be a goalkeeper since he was seven, but his gloves had split along the thumb two weeks before the district final. Mum had looked at the price in the sports shop, sighed quietly and said, "After payday, Leo. I promise." The final was on Saturday. Payday was the following Wednesday.

On Friday afternoon he sat on the bench beside the training pitch, turning the old gloves over in his hands. Sticky tape had lasted ten minutes of practice before peeling away like a banana skin. Across the grass, Rangga, the goalkeeper from the other team, was warming up. His gloves were bright orange and spotless.

"You're Leo, aren't you?" Rangga had wandered over, bouncing a ball on his knee. "I saw you save that penalty against Cahaya School. It was brilliant."

Leo shrugged. "Thanks. I might not play well tomorrow, though. My gloves are finished."

Rangga looked at the split thumb and whistled softly. Then he did something Leo did not expect. He dug into his kit bag and pulled out a second pair, grey and slightly faded, with a name written inside the cuff in black pen. "My brother's old ones," he said. "They're too big for me, so I never use them. Try them."

They fitted Leo almost perfectly. He caught the ball again and again, and it stuck to his palms as if it had been glued there.

"But we're playing against each other," Leo said slowly. "If I'm good tomorrow, your team might lose."

Rangga grinned. "Then I'll just have to be better. Where's the fun in beating a goalkeeper with broken gloves?"

Saturday's match was tight and noisy. Overnight rain had left puddles on one side of the pitch, and the ball skidded in strange directions. Leo dived left to keep out a hard shot, then stretched high to push another over the bar. At full time the score was one all, and the final went to penalties. Leo saved two of them, but Rangga saved three, and Leo's team lost four goals to three.

Leo stood very still, staring at the grass. Then a hand landed on his shoulder.

"Two saves," said Rangga, "in somebody else's gloves. I would not like to face you again."

Leo tried to hand the gloves back, but Rangga closed Leo's fingers around them. "Keep them until Wednesday," he said. "Then you can give them back, and we can have a rematch."

Leo laughed for the first time all day. It was hard to feel sad about losing to someone who had helped him play his best.
